Now let $\Phi=1 / r$, then applying Green's Theorem to the space
within the surface, and remembering that $\nabla^{2} \Phi=0$ and $\nabla^{2} \Psi=0$
throughout the limits of integration we find
$$\iint \Psi \frac{d \frac{1}{r}}{d \nu^{\prime}} d s-4 \pi \Psi_{P}=\iint \frac{1}{r} d \Psi \nu_{\nu^{\prime}} d s^{*}$$
(10)
where $\Psi_{P}$ is the value of $\Psi$ at $P$.
Again, if we apply the theorem to the space between the
surface $s$ and a surface surrounding it at an infinite distance $a$,
the part of the surface-integral belonging to the latter surface
will be of the order $1 / a$ and may be neglected, and we have
$$\iint \Psi^{\prime} \frac{d \frac{1}{r}}{d \nu} d s=\iint \frac{1}{r} d \Psi^{\prime} d s$$
(11)
Now at the surface, $\Psi=\Psi^{\prime}$, and since the normals $\nu$ and $\nu^{\prime}$ are
drawn in opposite directions,
$$\frac{d \frac{1}{r}}{d \nu}+\frac{d \frac{1}{r}}{d \nu^{\prime}}=0 .$$
Hence on adding equations (10) and (11), the left-hand mem-
bers destroy each other, and we have
$$-4 \pi \Psi_{P}=\iint \frac{1}{r}\left(\frac{d \Psi}{d v^{\prime}}+\frac{d \Psi^{\prime}}{d v}\right) d s$$
( ${ }^{12}$ )
97 b.] Green also proves that if the value of the potential $\Psi$
at every point of a closed surface $s$ be given arbitrarily, the
potential at any point inside or outside the surface may be
determined, provided $\nabla^{2} \Psi=0$ inside or outside the surface.
For this purpose he supposes the function $\Phi$ to be such that
near the point $P$ its value is sensibly $1 / r$, while at the surface
$s$ its value is zero, and at every point within the surface
$$\nabla^{2} \Phi=0$$

\end{equation*}$$

where $\Psi_{P}$ is the value of $\Psi$ at $P$.

 surface $s$ and a surface surrounding it at an infinite distance $a$,

 will be of the order $1 / a$ and may be neglected, and we have

$$\begin{equation*}
\iint \Psi^{\prime} \frac{d \frac{1}{r}}{d \nu} d s=\iint \frac{1}{r} d \Psi^{\prime} d s \tag{11}
\end{equation*}$$


Now at the surface, $\Psi=\Psi^{\prime}$, and since the normals $\nu$ and $\nu^{\prime}$ are

$$\frac{d \frac{1}{r}}{d \nu}+\frac{d \frac{1}{r}}{d \nu^{\prime}}=0 .$$


Hence on adding equations (10) and (11), the left-hand mem
bers destroy each other, and we have

$$\begin{equation*}
-4 \pi \Psi_{P}=\iint \frac{1}{r}\left(\frac{d \Psi}{d v^{\prime}}+\frac{d \Psi^{\prime}}{d v}\right) d s \tag{}
\end{equation*}$$


97 b.] Green also proves that if the value of the potential $\Psi$

 potential at any point inside or outside the surface may be
 determined, provided $\nabla^{2} \Psi=0$ inside or outside the surface.

 near the point $P$ its value is sensibly $1 / r$, while at the surface
 $s$ its value is zero, and at every point within the surface

$$\nabla^{2} \Phi=0$$
